article_content: Boris Johnson launched a fierce critique of a government adviser who rejected his vision for a massive four-runway airport in the Thames Estuary. Calling the commission’s decision a step backward for Britain’s aviation future, the London Mayor likened it to other shelved feasibility studies gathering dust in Whitehall. Still, Johnson insisted his proposal is far from dead, even though Sir Howard Davies’s team now plans to consider only three alternatives: two possibilities for Heathrow and one for Gatwick. Johnson argued that Heathrow’s limitations make the Estuary project the best chance for sustaining the UK’s competitiveness. But the Airports Commission has advised ministers to focus on expanding either Heathrow or Gatwick, rather than Johnson’s plan. Prior to the official announcement, Johnson assailed the move and predicted the verdict would get lost among numerous other neglected reports. Speaking on his LBC phone-in show, Johnson condemned enlarging Heathrow, claiming it would exacerbate a flawed 1950s planning decision and create new noise issues for areas not currently beneath flight paths. He blamed the setback on a lack of political will, not poor planning. Citing the Channel Tunnel, which was originally dismissed but later built, he remained optimistic about the Estuary concept. Critics outside City Hall, including the Labour Party, labeled the scheme an extravagant vanity project. Airline representatives echoed doubts over its location and massive expenses, insisting that development costs must be justified since they would ultimately be borne by airlines and passengers. With the Estuary proposal off the table, the Commission will finalize its choice among three airport expansion options by summer 2015. Johnson, undeterred, argued that brushing aside this visionary solution only prolongs the stale debate over Britain’s airport capacity.

article_content: New guidance from the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) states that some parents are 'in denial' about their children being obese, which may hinder successful weight management. Research indicates that 30% of youngsters are overweight or obese, leading to higher risks of conditions such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer in adulthood. NICE warns that family attitudes can undermine efforts to address childhood obesity, especially if there is a lack of understanding about lifestyle weight management programs. Figures show the NHS has spent £4 million on Weight Watchers courses since 2007, with two-thirds of local health authorities offering these programs. In England, around 30% of boys and girls aged two to 15, plus 23% of children in reception and 34% in year 6, are overweight or obese. NICE advises that families recognize the problem and commit to strategies like reading food labels and incorporating more physical activity into daily routines. Experts such as Tam Fry of the National Obesity Forum emphasize the need for proper funding at council levels to put these recommendations into practice. Professor Mike Kelly of NICE highlights that obesity can seriously affect a child's quality of life, self-esteem, and exposure to bullying, urging local commissioners to provide accessible services.

article_content: 'Louis van Gaal faces a £200 million dilemma before facing Southampton at Old Trafford on Sunday, forced to sit out at least one of his top attackers. After battling widespread injuries, Manchester United is finally near full strength with an 11-match unbeaten streak, so Van Gaal must carefully maintain balance among his star names.' 'The manager's 'famous five'—Wayne Rooney, Robin van Persie, Radamel Falcao, Angel di Maria, and Juan Mata—are all fit, prompting Van Gaal to hint that he will not play them all. He argues he can only accommodate four creative players effectively, assuring that quality, rather than rotation, guides his decisions.' 'Rooney remains almost certain to start, being club captain and on track to become United's all-time leading scorer. Van Persie, once untouchable, now faces increased competition. Falcao, hoping for a permanent deal, has proven his finishing ability but must demonstrate more beyond just scoring.' 'Mata, initially doubted under Van Gaal, has flourished as a playmaker. Meanwhile, Di Maria returned from injury to score against Yeovil, reinforcing the Dutch manager's options in attack. Despite Di Maria's record transfer fee, Van Gaal insists cost doesn't dictate selection.' 'With almost everyone healthy—Marcos Rojo, Daley Blind, Luke Shaw, Rafael, and Falcao are available—Van Gaal can shape his lineup as he pleases. While Ashley Young remains out, the manager is poised to continue a strong run, targeting further improvement both now and in future seasons.' 'He hasn't ruled out new faces in January if they offer immediate value, hinting at his pursuit of defenders like Matt Hummels. Regardless, he praises Southampton under Ronald Koeman for challenging the top four and anticipates a tough match, given their performance in December.' 'For Van Gaal, the real puzzle is deciding who among his four star forwards makes the cut, as Rooney, van Persie, Falcao, Di Maria, and Mata battle for a place in what he hopes will become a more attack-minded United side in the long run.'

article_content: A massive 8.6-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of the Indonesian island of Sumatra on Wednesday afternoon, prompting a tsunami watch for the Indian Ocean that was later canceled. The quake was centered about 434 kilometers southwest of Banda Aceh, at a depth of 23 kilometers, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. A second large quake, measuring 8.2, occurred about two hours later in the same region. Officials noted smaller quakes ranging from magnitude 5.1 to 5.4. No major destruction or deaths were reported, but four people were slightly injured on Simeulue Island, off the coast of Aceh. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center initially issued a tsunami watch, reporting a 1-meter wave near Meulaboh, Indonesia. Other areas saw waves of about a foot or less. British Prime Minister David Cameron offered assistance if needed. Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono said there were no immediate reports of significant damage or casualties in Aceh. Power outages occurred in Banda Aceh, prompting residents to seek higher ground. In Thailand, some coastal areas were evacuated as a precaution. Some Maldives resorts were also emptied, highlighting concerns of limited local warning systems. In 2004, a massive 9.1-magnitude underwater earthquake off Sumatra caused a devastating tsunami, killing more than 200,000 people across 14 countries, with Aceh province suffering heavily. Since then, officials have improved warning systems and conducted drills. Indonesia lies on the 'Ring of Fire,' prone to frequent quakes and volcanic eruptions. Wednesday's quake was largely horizontal in movement, decreasing the likelihood of a destructive tsunami. The tsunami watch was lifted hours later, and authorities confirmed the threat had passed.

article_content: This weekend’s full moon will seem bigger and brighter than usual, thanks to what astronomers call a super perigee moon — the largest in nearly two decades. According to the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, the last time the moon was this large and close to Earth was in March 1993. Due to the moon’s elliptical orbit, it is about 31,000 miles closer to Earth at perigee than at apogee. NASA notes that when the moon is at perigee, it can appear about 14% bigger and 30% brighter. This is enhanced by the moon illusion, which makes the low-hanging moon appear unusually large through trees, buildings, or other objects in the foreground. Geoff Chester of the U.S. Naval Observatory says it’s worth a look, especially as the full moon rises in the east at sunset. Despite appearing close, it is still about 211,600 miles (356,577 km) away from Earth. If you miss it, you’ll have to wait until 2029 to see another supermoon of this magnitude.
